Name: Adam
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. You've just taken on an allotment. What's that like for you, at the moment?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Nervous, if I'm honest. Which is daft, at my age. I went down on Saturday, first proper day with the key, and there's three of the old boys stood by the gate with their flasks. And they all stopped talking. I said good morning, and they said good morning back, and then nothing. Just watched me go up the path. I could feel them on the back of my neck all the way to the plot. And I thought, I know this. I've been here before. I felt like the new lad on his first day at the depot. Sixteen, overalls two sizes too big, and every man in the place looking at you to see if you're going to last the week.

Name: Adam
Transcript: The new lad at the depot. What was that like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Oh, they had you. First week they sent me to the stores for a tin of tartan paint. And a bucket of steam. I went, as well. Both times. The storeman kept a straight face and all, he gave me an empty bucket and told me to be quick before it went cold. But that's how it worked. Nobody talked to you, not properly, till you'd shown you could do a job. You kept your head down and you got on, and one day somebody asks you to pass him a spanner, and that's you. You're in. Nobody says it. You just know. Took me about four months, as I remember. So I suppose I've gone down there thinking it's the same. You don't walk in and start chatting. You get your head down. You let the work do the talking.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What made you put your name down for a plot?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Retiring, mainly. I finished at the depot fourteen months ago. Forty-one years, man and boy. And the first few weeks were grand, lie-ins, Pat bringing me a cup of tea, the paper. I thought, I could get used to this. Then you start to go a bit funny. We're on the ninth floor, the flats by the ring road, and I worked out one week I'd gone three days without seeing the sky properly. Not through a window, I mean. Properly. Three days. I'd never done that in my life. At the depot you're in and out of the yard all day, in all weathers, rain coming in sideways off the bus wash. You never think you'll miss that. So I wanted somewhere to be that wasn't indoors. Somewhere with a job waiting for me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Somewhere with a job waiting for you.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Aye. Pat's got her own routine, see. She's had it forty years while I've been at work. Her choir on a Tuesday, her sister on a Thursday, the market on a Saturday. And I'm in it now. I'm in the way of the hoover. I caught myself one morning following her into the kitchen, just to see what she was doing. Following my own wife round the flat. That's when I knew. She's good about it, she never says anything. But I can feel it. It's like when you've stripped an engine right down and put it all back together, and it runs lovely, sweet as you like, and there's one part left in your hand. And you stand there with it. Everything works without it. That's what retiring's been. I'm the part left over.

Name: Adam
Transcript: The part left over. What's that like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Not good. I'll be honest. I don't go in for moaning, but it's not good. You wake up and there's nothing that needs you. Nobody's going to ring if you don't turn up. Forty-one years, somebody would have rung. Half the time I was the one they rang, two in the morning sometimes, a bus broken down on the bypass and nobody else could find what was wrong with it. And then it stops, like that, a do in the social club and a card with everybody's names in, and you're just a man in a chair on the ninth floor. Watching the buses go round the ring road. I know every one of them. I could tell you what's wrong with half of them from the sound. So when the letter came from the allotments, after two years with my name down, I thought, right. That's a job. That'll need me.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What does the plot look like now?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Brambles, mostly. Brambles and that couch grass, the stuff with the white roots that goes on for ever. You pull one bit and it's attached to another bit three yards off. The chap before me gave up two years since, so it's had two years to do what it likes. There's an old bath at the bottom, full of green water. A shed with no door. I stood there with a brand new fork on Saturday and I didn't know where to start. I just stood. I'm not used to that, not knowing where to start. Then I thought, start at the corner nearest the path. So at least people could see I was trying. So that's what I did. I've cleared about a square, maybe three yards by three. It's not much. But you can see it from the gate.

Name: Adam
Transcript: So people could see you trying. Tell me about that.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Well, the chap from the committee, when he gave me the key, he said half the new ones give up by June. He said it friendly enough. Like it was the weather. But I'm not having that. I'm not going to be one that gives up by June. So I want them to see it, the old boys, every time they come through the gate. That corner getting bigger. A bit more every week. That's how you show them. You don't tell them. You let them see.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you make of the old boys?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: They're all right, I expect. There's a Frank, I think, and a Ken. Some of them have been there thirty years. They know every inch of the place, which plots flood, where the frost sits, who's got the best muck. I'd like to know what they know. But you don't ask. Not yet. You've not earned asking. You ask a man something your first week and he'll tell you, but he'll think less of you for it. That's how I see it, anyway. Pat says I'm making it harder than it needs to be. She says, just go and talk to them, they're only men with sheds. She might be right. But I can't do it. It's not how I was brought up.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And the digging itself. What's that like for you?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Hard. Harder than I thought. First Saturday I did two hours straight, didn't stop, didn't have a drink even, and on the Sunday I couldn't get out of the chair. Pat had to give me a hand up. My knees have done forty years on concrete floors, under buses, and they let me know about it. And my back. I felt about ninety. And I sat there on the Sunday with the telly on and I had a horrible thought. I thought, what if I can't do it. What if that's me now. A man who can't dig a bit of garden.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What if that's me now. What was that like, thinking that?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Frightening, a bit. You don't think about your body when it works, do you. It's just there, it does what it's told. I could lie under a bus all day on a creeper board and get up and go for a pint. Now it's started sending in its own bills. So I went back on the Tuesday and I did an hour. Then I sat down. Then another half hour. You pace yourself, like a job you can't rush. You don't force a seized bolt, you give it time. But I'll be honest, part of the reason I'm down there is to find out. I suppose that's what it is. I'm finding out what I've got left.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What do you think you'll find?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I don't know. That's the honest answer. I'd like to think there's a fair bit left. My dad dug his allotment till he was past eighty, by the railway, and he was a smaller man than me. But he'd never stopped, you see. He never had a year in a chair. I've had a year in a chair, and I think it's taken something off me that I didn't know it was taking. So I'll find out by June, I expect. Either the knees get used to it or they don't. Pat says go to the doctor. I'm not going to the doctor about digging. I'd feel a fool. Sitting in that waiting room with all the poorly people, saying I've hurt myself on a bramble patch.

Name: Adam
Transcript: And when you're there on your own, what's that like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Quiet. In a good way. On the Tuesday I had a flask of tea on an upturned bucket, and I just sat. Twenty minutes. A robin came and sat on the fork handle, bold as you like, waiting for me to turn something over for him. I turned a bit over for him, and all. You can hear the trains from there, and the ring road a long way off, but it's quiet. Nobody needs anything from me down there. At home I'm always about to be asked to move. Lift your feet up, I'm doing under there. Down there nobody's going to ask me to move. I've not done that in years, just sat. I didn't know I could.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Nobody needs anything from you. Earlier you said you wanted a job that would need you.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: Aye, well. Both, I suppose. I want the job, and I want nobody wanting me. That doesn't make much sense, does it. But the plot needs doing, and it doesn't need me, if you follow. It'll wait. It's waited two years. It doesn't mind if I sit on a bucket. It's not going to ring anybody. At the depot if you sat down somebody wanted to know why. Down there the brambles don't care either way.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What does Pat make of it?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: She's pleased. She bought me the flask. She said, that'll get you out from under me. She said it nice. She meant it nice. I think she's relieved, if I'm honest, and I don't blame her. She's had a year of me asking what's for tea at eleven in the morning. I'd not have minded her being a bit sorry, mind. Just a bit. But you can't have it both ways, can you. I've been under her feet a year. She's earned her kitchen back.

Name: Adam
Transcript: You'd not have minded her being a bit sorry.

Name: Hollis
Transcript: No. Forty-odd years married, you'd like to think you'd be missed a bit, even from under her feet. But she's got her life. She made it while I was at work, and she's right to keep it. It's me that has to make something now. That's the size of it. At sixty-eight I've got to make myself a life, and I've never had to before, because the depot was my life and it came ready made. You turned up and it was there. Nobody tells you that, when you retire. That you'll have to start again from nothing, like a lad.

Name: Adam
Transcript: What are you hoping the year will be like?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: I'm not one for hoping. I'd like some potatoes. My dad always had potatoes, earlies and main crop, and I'd like a sack of my own. I'd like to get to the back end of the year with the whole plot cleared, edge to edge, and that bath gone. And I'll tell you what I'd really like, since you ask. I'd like to walk through that gate one morning and have them carry on talking. Not stop. Just carry on, like I've always been there. That's all. I'd settle for that.

Name: Adam
Transcript: Thank you. Is there anything else about it, at the moment, that I haven't asked about?

Name: Hollis
Transcript: No, I think you've had it all. Only that I'm glad I did it. Nervous, like I said. Sore. But I'm glad. I went down this morning before I came here, just to look at it. Didn't do anything. Just looked at my square. You'd laugh. Three yards by three, and I stood there looking at it like it was a bus I'd rebuilt.
